## What the answer turned out to be

**Two states are

genuinely dangerous, not fifty.**

- **Illinois (BIPA)** — the only broad private right of action, $1,000/$5,000 per violation *plus plaintiff's attorneys' fees*, no har
m required, no size threshold. Mitigated but not eliminated: SB 2979 capped recovery at one per person per coll

ection method, and the 7th Circuit confirmed retroactivity in 2026.
- **Texas (CUBI)** — no private suits, but $25,000 per

violation uncapped and an AG who took **$1.4B off Meta**.

Then a manageable second tier: Washington (MHMD private right of action), Colorado

(45-day retention clock — strictest in the country), California, Maryland (the one state where consent can't cure a necessity failure).

## Three findings worth pulling out

**The
sleeper risk is California.** No biometric consent statute, so nobody watches it — but CCPA § 1798.150 gives private plaintiffs $100–$750 per consumer per incident for breaches of biometric data. A
stored template database is a standing class action waiting for one incident. It only reaches non-encrypted data, so encryption at rest is a real

defence.

**Your vendor doesn't absorb this.** Coinbase was sued in Illinois in May 2025 over precisely this architecture, and the pleaded theory is

that the template should have been destroyed after verification and wasn't. In the parallel Jumio case, Illinois jurisdiction attached on nothing more than the user being in Illinois when they submitted their licence and face.

**One dec

ision dominates everything else:** delete the template immediately after the match. It clears every retention clock simultaneously, satisfies Maryland's standard, removes the California target, and kills the theory currently being litigated against

your competitors. Cost is re-verification and face-based duplicate detection.

## Two things I deliberately did not paper over

I couldn't resolve wh
ether BIPA § 15(c)'s bar on "otherwise profiting from" biometric data reaches a subscription gated behind a face scan — courts are split and I'm not going to guess on the
one question that's specific to your business model. And my Washington read (that you fall inside MHMD's fraud-prevention exception) is
what puts Washington in Tier 2 rather than Tier 1; I couldn't confirm it against a primary source. Both are on the counsel brief as numbered questions, and I've flagged what chang

es if the Washington read is wrong.
